questions.stem: (a) Describe an activity to show that glucose and alcohol, although they contain hydrogen, are not acids. (b) What ion do acids produce in water, and in what form does it exist? questions.answer: (a) Fix two nails on a cork in a beaker and connect them through a bulb and switch to a 6 volt battery. Pour dilute HCl into the beaker and switch on — the bulb glows. (c) Dissolving an acid in water is highly exothermic. If water is added to concentrated acid, the heat may make the mixture splash out and cause burns, and the glass container may break from local heating; adding acid slowly to water with stirring prevents this. (d) Dilution decreases the concentration of H₃O⁺ ions per unit volume.

questions.stem: Zinc is a metal in the middle of the activity series. (a) Explain, with balanced equations, how zinc is obtained from its sulphide ore and from its carbonate ore. Name each step. (b) Why can metals such as sodium and aluminium not be obtained by heating their oxides with carbon, and how are they obtained instead?
questions.answer: (a) It is easier to obtain a metal from its oxide, so the ores are first converted to zinc oxide. Roasting — the sulphide ore is heated strongly in excess air: 2ZnS(s) + 3O₂(g) → 2ZnO(s) + 2SO₂(g). Calcination — the carbonate ore is heated strongly in limited air: ZnCO₃(s) → ZnO(s) + CO₂(g). Reduction — zinc oxide is heated with carbon: ZnO(s) + C(s) → Zn(s) + CO(g). (b) These metals are very reactive and have more affinity for oxygen than carbon has, so carbon cannot reduce their oxides. questions.stem: Describe the path of blood through the four chambers of the human heart. Why do ventricles have thicker walls than atria? What is double circulation, and why is it necessary in birds and mammals but not in fishes?
questions.answer: Oxygen-rich blood from the lungs enters the left atrium, which contracts and passes it to the left ventricle; the muscular left ventricle pumps it to the body. De-oxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium, then the right ventricle, which pumps it to the lungs for oxygenation. Valves prevent backflow. Ventricles have thicker muscular walls because they pump blood out to various organs. Double circulation: blood passes through the heart twice in each cycle — once for the lungs and once for the body. Keeping the right and left sides separate prevents mixing of oxygenated and de-oxygenated blood and gives a highly efficient oxygen supply, which birds and mammals need because they constantly use energy to maintain body temperature. Fishes have a two-chambered heart; blood goes to the gills, is oxygenated and passes directly to the body, so it goes through the heart only once.

questions.stem: Explain how the level of sugar in the blood is kept under control by a feedback mechanism. Why are some patients of diabetes given injections of insulin?
questions.answer: Insulin, produced by the pancreas, regulates blood sugar level. When the blood sugar level rises, this is detected by cells of the pancreas, which respond by producing more insulin; as the blood sugar level falls, insulin secretion is reduced. This is feedback control of the timing and amount of hormone released. In diabetes insulin is not secreted in proper amounts, so the blood sugar level rises and causes harmful effects; insulin injections supply the missing hormone and help bring the sugar level down.

questions.stem: A child accidentally touches a hot iron and pulls the hand away at once, before feeling the pain. (a) Trace the sequence of events in this reflex action, naming each part of the reflex arc. (b) Why is the reflex arc formed in the spinal cord and not in the brain? (c) Does the brain receive any information about this event?
questions.answer: (a) Receptors in the skin detect the heat (stimulus) → a sensory neuron carries the impulse to the spinal cord → in the spinal cord the impulse is passed through a relay neuron to a motor neuron → the motor neuron carries it to the effector, the arm muscles → the muscles contract and the hand is withdrawn. (b) Thinking in the brain involves complex interactions of many neurons and is too slow; the child could be burnt by then. Nerves from all over the body meet in a bundle in the spinal cord on their way to the brain, so connecting the input and output nerves there gives a quick response. (c) Yes — the information input also goes on to reach the brain, which is how the child later feels the pain and becomes aware of what happened.

questions.stem: (a) Which hormone prepares the body of an animal to fight or run away in a scary situation? Name the gland that secretes it and describe three effects it has on the body. (b) Give two limitations of electrical impulses as a means of communication, and explain why chemical coordination by hormones overcomes them.
questions.answer: (a) Adrenaline, secreted by the adrenal glands directly into the blood. Effects: the heart beats faster, supplying more oxygen to the muscles; blood supply to the digestive system and skin is reduced by contraction of muscles around small arteries, diverting blood to the skeletal muscles; the breathing rate increases because of contractions of the diaphragm and rib muscles. (b) Electrical impulses reach only cells connected by nervous tissue, not every cell; and once a cell has generated and transmitted an impulse it needs time to reset before it can send another, so cells cannot create impulses continually. Hormones released into the blood diffuse and can reach all cells regardless of nervous connections, and can act steadily and persistently, though more slowly.

Three effects: heart rate, blood diverted to muscles, faster breathing

questions.passage: Kabir filled a conical flask with water, covered its neck with wire mesh and placed three freshly germinated bean seeds on the mesh. He kept the flask inside a cardboard box open on one side only, with the open side facing a window. After three days the shoots had bent towards the window and the roots had bent away from it. He then turned the flask round so that the shoots faced away from the light, and left it for a few more days. The older bent parts did not straighten, but the new growth of the shoots turned towards the window again. He also noticed that the roots kept growing downwards into the water.

questions.stem: How is pollination different from fertilisation in flowering plants?
questions.answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the stamen (anther) to the stigma — in the same flower (self-pollination) or to another flower (cross-pollination) by wind, water or animals. Fertilisation is the fusion of the male germ-cell from the pollen grain with the female gamete (egg) in the ovule, after a pollen tube grows through the style to the ovary; it produces the zygote.

questions.stem: What is vegetative propagation? Give three advantages of growing plants such as sugarcane, roses or grapes by this method.
questions.answer: Vegetative propagation is the development of new plants from parts such as the root, stem or leaves under appropriate conditions, used in methods such as layering or grafting. Advantages: plants raised this way bear flowers and fruits earlier than those produced from seeds; plants such as banana, orange, rose and jasmine that have lost the capacity to produce seeds can be propagated; all plants produced are genetically similar enough to the parent to have all its characteristics.

questions.stem: How does the developing embryo get nourishment inside the mother's body? How are its wastes removed?
questions.answer: After implantation in the uterine lining, the embryo gets nutrition from the mother's blood through a special tissue, the placenta, a disc embedded in the uterine wall. It has villi on the embryo's side, surrounded by blood spaces on the mother's side, which provide a large surface area for glucose and oxygen to pass from the mother to the embryo. Waste substances generated by the embryo are transferred into the mother's blood through the placenta.

questions.stem: Why is variation beneficial to a species but not necessarily to an individual? Illustrate with the example of bacteria living in temperate waters.
questions.answer: Variation may not help a particular individual — some variations are so drastic that the new cell cannot work and dies. But a population is suited to its niche, and niches can change for reasons beyond the organisms' control. If some individuals carry variations, there is a chance that they survive the change, so the species survives. For example, if the water temperature of bacteria living in temperate waters rose because of global warming, most of the bacteria would die, but the few variants resistant to heat would survive and grow further.

questions.stem: (a) Name the three parts of the pistil and state the function of the ovary. (b) Distinguish between unisexual and bisexual flowers with one example of each. (c) Describe the events from the landing of a pollen grain on the stigma to the formation of seed and fruit.
questions.answer: (a) Stigma (terminal, may be sticky), style (middle elongated part) and ovary (swollen bottom part). The ovary contains ovules, each with an egg cell. (b) A unisexual flower contains either stamens or pistil, e.g. papaya or watermelon; a bisexual flower contains both, e.g. Hibiscus or mustard. (c) A pollen tube grows out of the pollen grain and travels through the style to reach the ovary. The male germ-cell fuses with the female gamete in the ovule (fertilisation), forming a zygote. The zygote divides several times to form an embryo within the ovule. The ovule develops a tough coat and becomes a seed; the ovary grows rapidly and ripens into a fruit, while petals, sepals, stamens, style and stigma may shrivel and fall off.

questions.stem: (a) Trace the path of the egg in the human female reproductive system from its release to implantation, if it is fertilised. (b) How does the uterus prepare each month to receive a fertilised egg? (c) What happens if the egg is not fertilised?
questions.answer: (a) One egg is produced every month by one of the ovaries. It is carried from the ovary towards the uterus through the thin oviduct (fallopian tube). Sperms entering through the vagina travel up to the oviduct, where fertilisation may occur. The fertilised egg (zygote) starts dividing to form a ball of cells, the embryo, which is implanted in the lining of the uterus, where it grows and develops organs to become a foetus. (b) Every month the lining of the uterus thickens, becomes spongy and is richly supplied with blood to nourish an embryo. (c) If the egg is not fertilised it lives for about one day. The thickened lining is no longer needed, so it slowly breaks down and comes out through the vagina as blood and mucus. This cycle, called menstruation, occurs roughly every month and usually lasts about two to eight days.

questions.passage: For a science project, Anika kept a wet slice of bread in a cool, moist, dark cupboard. Within a few days thread-like white structures spread over its surface, and tiny black blobs on thin stalks appeared among them. At the same time she cut a potato into small pieces, some with a notch (an eye) and some without, and placed them on moist cotton in a tray. After a week, green shoots and roots had grown only from the pieces that had notches. Her teacher told her that both the bread mould and the potato had produced new individuals from a single parent.

parts.prompt: The tiny black blobs on stalks on the bread are
parts.answer: (a) — the blobs are sporangia; the thread-like structures are hyphae, which are not reproductive.

parts.prompt: How are the spores of the bread mould able to survive until they reach a suitable place to grow?
parts.answer: They are covered by thick walls that protect them until they come into contact with another moist surface.

parts.prompt: Why did only the potato pieces with notches grow? Name this mode of reproduction and the general name for reproduction from a single parent.
parts.answer: The notches contain buds, which give rise to new shoots and roots; pieces without buds cannot (1 mark). This is vegetative propagation (½), a form of asexual reproduction (½).
